title: Symptom-Level Comorbidity Patterns Between Depression and Internet Gaming Disorder Among Adolescents: Evidence from Longitudinal Network Analysis with Gender Considerations
authors: Shiyun Chen, Yue Zhao, Xinli Chi, Shimin Zhu
abstract: Adolescence is a period with an increased risk for the co-occurrence of depression and Internet gaming disorder (IGD), yet we still know little about how specific symptoms of these two conditions influence each other over time. In this study, we applied cross-lagged panel network analysis to two-wave data from a community sample of 538 adolescents (Mean age = 12.51 years; 53.7 percent female). Potential gender differences in the network structure were examined. In the overall sample and in both gender groups, depressive symptoms consistently predicted later gaming-related problems, whereas no reverse cross-disorder pathways were retained. In particular, suicidal ideation and psychomotor symptoms emerged as bridge symptoms linking depression and IGD, while sleep problems showed moderate outgoing expected influence in the overall symptom network. While boys and girls showed broadly similar patterns, some differences emerged in how specific symptoms were connected and which symptoms were most influential. These findings clarify the longitudinal symptom-level associations between depression and IGD in adolescents, suggesting that addressing key depressive symptoms may help reduce the risk of later IGD.

title: Scripts of Escalation and Restraint: State Messaging and Public Opinion in International Crises
authors: Frances Yaping Wang
abstract: Public opinion can both enable and constrain foreign policy, motivating governments to manipulate media during international crises. This study identifies four recurring communication strategies, one mobilizing and three moderating, each organized around a dominant cue: mobilization relies primarily on emotional arousal to stoke nationalist sentiment and foster assertiveness; censorship centers on the informational restriction of politically sensitive content; delegitimization uses normative appeals to discredit hawkish responses as irresponsible or illegitimate; and posturing employs performative displays of toughness intended to make moderate policies politically acceptable. Using a large-scale survey experiment in China, Vietnam, and the Philippines, the study evaluates how these strategies affect the public’s foreign-policy preferences and tolerance for policy deviation in a simulated fishing dispute in the South China Sea. The results show that mobilization shifts preferences in a more hawkish direction and reduces tolerance for deviation, whereas delegitimization consistently steers the public toward more moderate foreign policy preferences across countries. Censorship tempers policy preferences in all three countries but is strongest in Vietnam; posturing has no significant effect in China or Vietnam and produces a more hawkish response in the Philippines. Although the sources of this cross-national heterogeneity cannot be definitively identified, the findings suggest that propaganda effectiveness may depend partly on how audiences interpret different messages. Explicitly prescriptive strategies, such as mobilization and delegitimization, appear more portable across contexts, whereas informational or performative strategies, such as censorship and posturing, may be more contingent on audience predispositions, including baseline hawkishness, and on broader political and informational environments.

title: Can citizen election observation increase public confidence in US elections?
authors: Jennie Barker, Oren Samet, Susan D. Hyde
abstract: Nonpartisan citizen election observation plays an important role in promoting the credibility of electoral processes around the world. This article assesses whether nonpartisan observation can shape attitudes among the US public, randomizing information about nonpartisan domestic observers in a series of survey experiments fielded to nearly 10,000 respondents. These included both hypothetical vignettes and information about a real‐world nonpartisan domestic observation mission undertaken by The Carter Center during the 2022 midterm elections in Fulton County, Georgia. The results show that information about positive assessments by nonpartisan observers of the hypothetical and Fulton County elections increased respondents' confidence in electoral results and processes, and also made respondents more likely to identify the officially announced winner over the candidate they favored as the candidate who won. Alternative ways of framing observers were largely inconsequential.

title: How Accurate Are Survey Measurements of Objective Phenomena?
authors: Lisanne Wichgers, Linchiat Chang, David Chapman, Elizabeth Elder, Jon Krosnick, Matt Berent, Amanda Scott, Elaine Albertson, Elizabeth Quinlan
abstract: How accurate are survey measurements of phenomena that can be objectively verified? This article reports a review of various types of evidence assessing accuracy (vs. benchmarks not derived from self-reports) across a wide spectrum of content areas, including demographics, healthcare, labor force statistics, substance use and more. The vast majority of measurements were accurate, according to three assessment methods. Individual respondents’ self-reports closely matched objective records of the same phenomena for the same individual. Small aggregate differences were observed between survey sample means and aggregate means derived from objective records. Self-reports correlated strongly with measures of the same attributes of those individuals from secondary data not based on self-reports. Taken together, the evidence suggests that survey measurements of objective phenomena are highly accurate.

title: An Image Is Worth K Topics: A Visual Structural Topic Model with Pretrained Image Embeddings
authors: Matías Piqueras, Alexandra Segerberg, Matteo Magnani, Måns Magnusson, Nataša Sladoje
abstract: Political scientists are increasingly interested in analyzing visual content at scale. However, the existing computational toolbox is still in need of methods and models attuned to the specific challenges and goals of social and political inquiry. In this article, we introduce a visual structural topic model (vSTM) that combines continuous image embeddings with a structural topic model. This has important advantages compared to existing approaches. First, continuous embeddings allow the model to capture the semantic complexity of images, which is relevant to the study of politics. A consequence of using continuous embeddings is that we can directly use off-the-shelf pretrained deep learning models, offering state-of-the-art performance in image analysis tasks while saving time, cost and resources. Second, the structural topic model provides the ability to analyze how topics and covariates are related, while maintaining a nuanced representation of images as a mixture of multiple topics. In our experiments, we show that the vSTM is able to identify topics that are interpretable, coherent and relevant to the study of online political communication.

title: Political trust in crisis? An experimental panel study into the origins of subjective perceptions of structurally declining political trust
authors: H Bey, T W G van der Meer
abstract: The perception that political trust is in a deep crisis, driven by structurally declining trends, seems intrinsically tied to democracy. For decades, scholars responded by studying actual trends. Yet, actual trends can only partially explain the prevalence of the trust crisis narrative. Therefore, this study shifts the focus to perceived trends by comparing the actual longitudinal changes in political trust with citizens’ retrospective perceptions of these changes. We rely on observational and novel experimental data (n = 1882) from the Dutch LISS panel to investigate these incongruencies between actual trends and perceptions over a 16-year period (2008–2024). We find evidence for a bias in public opinion as past levels of trust are generally overestimated. By probing explanations from political science, sociology, and psychology, we find that this bias is primarily political rather than personal: how people remember their trust depends on whether their party governed, and reminding them who did corrects that memory.
journal_full: International Journal of Public Opinion Research

title: Who Goes Toxic? Understanding Political Toxicity on Social Media Across Individuals and Contexts
authors: Alon Zoizner, Nir Lotan, Sagi Pendzel, Einat Minkov
abstract: As political toxicity has become widespread on social media, scholars have sought to understand what drives it. While studies often emphasize platform-level explanations, such as algorithmic amplification, they offer limited insight into which users are more likely to produce toxic content. Even less is known about how the relationship between individual-level factors and toxicity varies across political contexts. Using data from 184,354 randomly sampled U.S. Twitter (now X) users, their original tweets (25M), and the accounts they follow, we link users’ inferred characteristics and political context to their real-life toxic behavior. Results show that Republican, male, and older users are consistently more likely to post both impolite and intolerant content, whereas education shows no clear association. We also find that state-level electoral competitiveness increases overall toxicity and, in some cases, conditions individual-level relationships. The age gap in impolite behavior significantly narrows in more competitive states, while the corresponding moderation for intolerance is only marginally significant. There is also some indication that partisan differences in impoliteness become larger in more competitive states, but this moderation is only marginally significant. Together, these results demonstrate that political toxicity is shaped jointly by users’ individual characteristics and the political contexts in which they operate.

title: Automating Abstract Screening in Research Synthesis Using Large Language Models: A Tutorial and Proof-of-Concept Study
authors: Mirka Henninger, Jan Radek, Jean-Paul Snijder-Steinhilber, Martin Pauly
abstract: Screening abstracts is a crucial yet labor-intensive step in research-synthesis projects, such as systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Large language models (LLMs) promise an opportunity to streamline and automate this process. However, there is still little guidance and practical insight into how such automated workflows can be implemented in research practice. In this article, we propose, describe, and illustrate an abstract-screening procedure using LLMs including a quantification of uncertainty of model outputs. We provide a step-by-step tutorial in which we address how to select an LLM, access LLMs from within R, develop and refine suitable prompts, define structured output formats, and describe whether and how model hyperparameters should be set. We then illustrate this procedure in a proof-of-concept study using a set of human-rated abstracts from a recent meta-analysis for comparison. We demonstrate that LLM-assisted screening can substantially reduce the time and cost of review preparation while maintaining accuracy comparable with human raters. To support psychological researchers in adopting LLM-based workflows for research synthesis, we also provide R scripts and implementation guidance on Gitlab. At the same time, we emphasize that this work represents an initial step and that continued refinement and validation are essential given that LLM technologies and their applications continue to evolve rapidly.
journal_full: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science

title: The news we use: A systematic scoping review of fake news stimuli in psychological research
authors: Theodore C. Webster, Ariana Modirrousta-Galian, Faye C. Skelton, Marina C. Wimmer
abstract: Research into fake news has surged in popularity, with over 3,000 publications on the topic each year since 2021. Definitions of what constitutes “fake news” vary across the field of psychology, where source, number, content, and presentation of stimuli may all be different yet still described as “fake news.” Thus, conclusions drawn from fake news research may only generalize to the particular definition or presentation of fake news used in a given study. Relatedly, stimuli may not be available or described clearly enough for reproducibility. To assess the scope of these potential issues, we conducted and reported a PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses) systematic scoping review of three databases including the last 11 years of psychology studies that used fake news stimuli. From the 881 included studies, we extracted and described the number, source, standardization, framing, and availability of fake news stimuli. Our findings suggest a large degree of stimuli variability, with high rates of example and full set availability. Most frequently, research stimuli were about politics and were framed as a social media post, and examples were given in-text. We also evaluated ratios of real to fake news stimuli, where an equal number of real and fake articles was the most frequent ratio. We recommend continued transparency, offering suggestions for open science practices following copyright law and considerations of generalizability regarding fake news in research.

title: Increasing Support for Humanitarian Aid to Palestinian Civilians During the Israel–Gaza War Through Ideologically Tailored Social-Media Campaigns
authors: Nimrod Nir, Eran Halperin
abstract: Promoting support for humanitarian aid to an adversarial outgroup is difficult during active war. We introduce a digital field-experimental approach that embeds psychologically grounded interventions in people’s actual social-media environments. During the Israel–Gaza war, 6,105 adult Jewish Israeli Facebook users were assigned to a no-study-campaign control condition, a humanitarian-moral campaign emphasizing humanitarian obligation, or an instrumental-security campaign presenting aid as advancing Israeli security. Days after the campaigns ended, 4,784 participants completed the follow-up survey. Support for humanitarian aid declined in the control condition but increased under both campaigns, suggesting that psychological social-media interventions can buffer or reverse erosion of humanitarian attitudes during acute conflict. Political ideology moderated relative effectiveness: the instrumental-security campaign was especially effective among conservatives, whereas liberals responded positively to both. These findings provide partial support for ideological message matching and offer a scalable, ecologically valid framework for testing intergroup interventions in real-world settings.
